blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Chemical equilibrium in chemistry revolves around the dynamic balance that occurs in a reversible chemical reaction when the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal.

  • Chemical equilibrium is temperature-dependent.
  • It applies only to closed systems where no substances are added or removed.
  • It is a state of maximum entropy and minimum Gibbs free energy for the system.

blocks.title: Chemical Reaction
blocks.text:
Chemical reaction: Symbolic representation of any chemical change in terms of reactants and products is called a chemical reaction.

On the Basis of Heat

• Endothermic reaction:

The reaction in which heat is absorbed is called as an endothermic reaction.

ΔH = +ve

• Exothermic reaction:

The reaction in which heat is evolved is called as an exothermic reaction.

ΔH = -ve and ΔH < 0

On the Basis of Direction

• Reversible reaction

Proceed in forward as well as in backward direction.

• Irreversible reaction

Proceed only in one direction (forward direction).

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Chemical Equilibrium

At equilibrium state

• Rate of forward reaction ($r_f$)= Rate of backward reaction ($r_b$)

• The concentration of the reactants and products does not change with time.

• At this stage, number of moles of substances produced per second in the forward reaction is equal to the number of moles of substances which disappear per second in the backward reaction.
Active Mass

The term active mass means the concentration of the reactants expressed in moles per litre (molar concentration) or the pressure of the reacting gas in atmosphere. In the case of gases and solutions, the molar concentration means the number of gram molecules present per litre.

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{\text{Number of gram moles of the substance}}{\text{Volume (in liters)}}$

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{Weight of substance(in grams)}{Molecular weight (MM) \times Volume (in L)}$

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{W \times 1000}{(MM) \times V(mL)}$

Homogeneous Equilibrium:

  • Definition: In homogeneous equilibrium, all the reactants and products are in the same phase (either all gases, all liquids, or all solids).
  • Example: The equilibrium between nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄) in the gas phase:
$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$

Heterogeneous Equilibrium:

  • Definition: In heterogeneous equilibrium, the reactants and products are in different phases (e.g., solid, liquid, or gas).
  • Example: The equilibrium between calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$) and its decomposition products:
$\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$the

blocks.title: Dalton’s Law
blocks.text:
Partial Pressure

It is the pressure of an individual gas in the gaseous mixture.

Dalton’s Law

It states that the total pressure of any gas mixture is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of each gas present in the mixture at a constant temperature and volume.

Let us consider a mixture of 3 gases A, B and C

According to Dalton’s Law:

$P_T = P_A + P_B + P_C$

Partial pressure of gas = Mole fraction × Total pressure

blocks.title: Law of Mass Action
blocks.text:
• It states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of active masses of the reacting substances raised to the power equal to the stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced chemical equation.

for the given equation:

$m_1A + m_2B \to n_1C + n_2D$

$\huge\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\left(P_C\right)^{n_1}\left(P_D\right)^{n_2}}{\left(P_A\right)^{m_1}\left(P_B\right)^{m_2}}$

$\huge\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{\mathrm{n}_1}[\mathrm{D}]^{\mathrm{n}_2}}{[\mathrm{A}]^{\mathrm{m}_1}[\mathrm{B}]^{\mathrm{m}_2}}
$

Relation between KP and KC

$K_p = K_c \left( RT \right)^{\Delta ng}$

Δ$n_g$=∑(Number of gaseous moles of product –∑ (Number of gaseous moles of reactants)

$\text{Units of } K_c = \text{mol}^{\Delta ng} \cdot \text{L}^{-\Delta ng}$

$\text{Units of } K_p = \text{atm}^{\Delta ng}$

Key point:

$K = \frac{K_f}{K_b}$

$\text{If } K > 1: $ Equilibrium favors the products (products are more stable).

$\text{If } K < 1: $ Equilibrium favors the reactants (reactants are more stable).

blocks.title: Reaction Quotient (Q)
blocks.text:
Consider a general homogeneous reversible reaction:

$m_1 A + m_2 B \rightleftharpoons n_1 C + n_2 D$

$\text{Reaction Quotient (Q):} \quad Q = \frac{[C]^{n_1} [D]^{n_2}}{[A]^{m_1} [B]^{m_2}}$

(at any t-time)

$\text{Equilibrium Constant (K):} \quad K = \frac{[C]^{n_1} [D]^{n_2}}{[A]^{m_1} [B]^{m_2}}$

(at equilibrium)

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: 2 moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas and 8 moles of $\text{CH}_4$ gas are present in a closed container at a total pressure of 2 atm. Calculate the partial pressure of $\text{H}_2$  and $\text{CH}_4$.
blocks.answer:
$\text{Given:} \quad P_{\text{total}} = 2 \, \text{atm}, \quad n_{\text{H}_2} = 2 \, \text{mol}, \quad n_{\text{CH}_4} = 8 \, \text{mol}$

$\chi_{\text{H}_2} = \frac{n_{\text{H}_2}}{n_{\text{total}}} = \frac{2}{2 + 8} = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2$

$\chi_{\text{CH}_4} = \frac{n_{\text{CH}_4}}{n_{\text{total}}} = \frac{8}{2 + 8} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8$

$P_{\text{H}_2} = \chi_{\text{H}_2} \times P_{\text{total}} = 0.2 \times 2 \, \text{atm} = 0.4 \, \text{atm}$

$P_{\text{CH}_4} = \chi_{\text{CH}_4} \times P_{\text{total}} = 0.8 \times 2 \, \text{atm} = 1.6 \, \text{atm}$

$\text{Partial pressure of } \text{H}_2 = 0.4 \, \text{atm}, \quad \text{Partial pressure of } \text{CH}_4 = 1.6 \, \text{atm}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Always check whether, deal with a system at equilibrium and use the correct expressions for Q (reaction quotient) or K (equilibrium constant).
  • Be mindful of the units and stoichiometric coefficients in equilibrium expressions.
  • temperature affect equilibrium constant, but pressure and concentration does not affect equilibrium constant.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
The core concept of dissociation in chemical equilibrium revolves around the reversible breakdown of a compound ( molecular substance) into simpler entities like  smaller molecules. This dissociation process occurs in a solution, and the system reaches an equilibrium where the rate of dissociation equals the rate of recombination.

For any chemical equilibrium dissociation always calculate in terms of mole. It is denoted by x.

blocks.title: Degree of Dissociation and Percentage Dissociation
blocks.text:
Degree of Dissociation:

It is the fraction of moles of reactant dissociated

$\alpha = \frac{x}{a_0}$

Percentage Dissociation:

It is the percentage fraction of moles of reactant dissociated.

$\alpha = \frac{x}{a_0}\times 100$

Where:

  • α = Degree of dissociation

blocks.title: Calculation of degree of dissociation from Vapour Density
tags: relation between degree of dissociation and molecular mass
relation between degree of dissociation and vapor density
blocks.text:
Relation in between degree of dissociation and Molecular mass:

$\alpha = \frac{[MW_{th} - MW_{obs}]}{MW_{obs}} \cdot \frac{n_1}{\Delta n_g}$

$\alpha$ = Degree of dissociation

$\text{MW}_{\text{th}}$ = Molecular weight of reactant also called as Theoretical Molecular Weight ($\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$)

$\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$ = Molecular weight of equilibrium mixture ($\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$)  also called as Observed Molecular Weight ($\text{MW}_{\text{obs}}$)

$\Delta n_g = \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of products} - \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of reactants}$

Relation between degree of dissociation and Vapour Density:

$\alpha = \left(\frac{D - d}{d}\right) \cdot \frac{n_1}{\Delta n_g}$

D = Initial vapour density ( Vapour density of reactant/Theoretical Vapour Density)

d = Vapour density at equilibrium

$\Delta n_g = \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of products} - \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of reactants}$

Moles of gas on reactants side

$n_1$ = Total initial moles of reactant

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
For a reaction AB↔A+B, the initial moles of AB are 3 moles. If 1 mole of AB dissociates, what is the percentage of dissociation?

1) 10%
2) 25%
3) 33%
4) 50%
blocks.answer:
The initial moles of AB are 3 moles.

If 1 mole of AB dissociates, the degree of dissociation α is:

$\alpha = \frac{\text{Amount dissociated}}{\text{Initial moles}} = \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.33$

$\text{Percentage Dissociation} = \alpha \times 100 = 0.33 \times 100 = 33.3\%$

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
$\text{PCl}_5(g) \leftrightharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$

The given reaction started with certain quantity of $\text{PCl}_5$. The mole fraction formed of$\text{Cl}_2$ at equilibrium is 0.25 and the pressure of the equilibrium mixture is 4 atm. Determine partial pressure of $\text{PCl}_3$ at equilibrium.

1) 1 atm
2) 2 atm
3) 3 atm
4) 4 atm
blocks.answer:
Given Reaction:

$\text{PCl}_5 \leftrightharpoons \text{PCl}_3 + \text{Cl}_2$

Initial Conditions at t=0:

$\text{PCl}_5: a \, \text{moles}, \quad \text{PCl}_3: 0 \, \text{moles}, \quad \text{Cl}_2: 0 \, \text{moles}$

At Equilibrium (t=teq)

$\text{PCl}_5: a - x, \quad \text{PCl}_3: x, \quad \text{Cl}_2: x$

Total Moles at Equilibrium:

$n_{\text{total}} = a - x + x + x = a + x$

Mole Fraction of $\text{Cl}_2$ at Equilibrium:

Given that the mole fraction of $\text{Cl}_2$ is 0.25:

=$\frac{x}{a + x} = 0.25 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \frac{0.25a}{0.75} = \frac{1}{3}a$

$\text{Mole fraction of } \text{PCl}_3 = \frac{x}{a + x} = 0.25 \quad \Rightarrow \quad P_{\text{PCl}_3} = 0.25 \times 4 = 1 \, \text{atm}$

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.question:
$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \leftrightharpoons 2\text{NO}_2$ The given reaction starts with 5 moles of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$. At equilibrium moles of $NO_
2$ are found to be double that of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.  Determine $K_C$ if the volume of the container is 500 mL.

1) 10 $\text{mol} \, \text{L}^{-1}$

2) 20 $\text{mol} \, \text{L}^{-1}$

3) 30 $\text{mol} \, \text{L}^{-1}$

4) 40 $\text{mol} \, \text{L}^{-1}$
blocks.answer:
$\mathrm{N_2O_4 (g) \rightleftharpoons 2 NO_2 (g)}$

Given Data:

  • Initial moles of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ = 5 moles
  • At equilibrium, moles of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ are double those of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$.
  • Volume of the container = 500 mL = 0.5 L
  • Define the changes in moles at equilibrium
Let the number of moles of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ that dissociate be x. From the stoichiometry of the reaction, for every 1 mole of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ that dissociates, 2 moles of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ are produced. Therefore, the equilibrium moles of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ are 2x, and the equilibrium moles of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ are 5−x.

• Use the given information about the mole ratio

We are told that at equilibrium, the moles of $NO_2$ are double those of $N_2O_4$​. Therefore:

2x=2(5−x)

x=2.5   moles of$N_2O_4$ ​dissociated.

Moles of $N_2O_4$ at equilibrium = 5−2.5=2.5 moles

Moles of $NO_2$ at equilibrium = 2x=2(2.5)=5 moles

$\left[ \mathrm{N_2O_4} \right] = \frac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume}} = \frac{2.5}{0.5} = 5 \, \text{M}$

$\left[ \mathrm{NO_2} \right] = \frac{\text{moles}}{\text{volume}} = \frac{5}{0.5} = 10 \, \text{M}$

The equilibrium constant expression for the reaction is:

$K_C = \frac{[\mathrm{N_2O_4}]}{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}$

$K_C = \frac{10^2}{(5)} = \frac{100}{5} = 20 \, \text{mol}^{} \, \text{L}^{-1}$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• The degree of dissociation (α) is the fraction of the original substance that dissociates. It's usually expressed as a ratio, ranging from 0 to 1 (0<α<1)
    • Percentage dissociation is the degree of dissociation multiplied by 100.
    • In heterogeneous equilibria (where multiple phases are present), the concentrations of pure solids and liquids do not appear in the equilibrium expression. A mistake is including the concentrations of pure solids or liquids, which are effectively constant.
    • When calculating vapour density for a dissociating substance, the observed vapor density is based on the substance's molar mass after dissociation.
    • Vapour density is half the molar mass of a gas, but students sometimes confuse it with molecular mass. The relationship between vapour density and molar mass must be remembered: VD=MM/2.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Chemical equilibrium is influenced by changes in concentration, pressure, and temperature, as explained by Le Chatelier's Principle: When a system at equilibrium experiences a disturbance, the system adjusts to partially counteract the disturbance and re-establish equilibrium.

• Le Chatelier's Principle states that when a dynamic equilibrium in a chemical system is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the system will respond by shifting the equilibrium position to counteract the disturbance and partially restore balance.

Shifts toward fewer gaseous moles (to lower pressure).
Shifts toward more gas moles (to increase pressure).
Shifts toward more gaseous moles (to fill space).
Shifts toward fewer gas moles (to reduce pressure).
Shifts toward more gas moles (to adjust pressure).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
For a reaction, $N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \leftrightharpoons 2NH_3(g); \, \Delta H = -\text{ve}$, then, determine the effect at equilibrium due to following changes:

(1) Decreasing concentration of H2

(2) Increasing the pressure

(3) Decreasing the temperature

(4) Catalyst

(5) Increasing the volume
blocks.answer:
1) Decreasing concentration of  $\text{H}_2$:

  • Decreasing  $\text{H}_2$  concentration reduces the availability of reactants.
  • Effect: The equilibrium shifts left (toward reactants) to produce more $\text{H}_2$​   . (Backward )
(2) Increasing the pressure:

  • Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas to reduce pressure.
  • Effect: The equilibrium shifts right (toward products) to form more $\text{NH}_3$. (Forward )
(3) Decreasing the temperature:

  • This is an exothermic reaction, where heat is a "product."
  • Decreasing the temperature removes heat, so the equilibrium shifts to produce more heat.
  • Effect: The equilibrium shifts right (toward products) to form more $\text{NH}_3$​. ( Forward)
(4) Catalyst:

  • A catalyst lowers the activation energy and increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally.
  • It does not affect the position of equilibrium; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster.
  • Effect: No change in equilibrium position. (No effect )
(5) Increasing the volume:

  • Increasing volume decreases pressure, and the system shifts to increase the number of gas molecules to restore balance.
  • More moles of gas are present on the reactant side (4 moles vs. 2 moles).
  • Effect: The equilibrium shifts left  toward reactants. (Backward)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming pressure affects equilibria for all reactions, but pressure only affects gaseous reactions where there is a difference in the number of moles of gas on either side of the equilibrium. If the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, changing pressure has no effect.
    • Incorrectly assuming that an increase in temperature always shifts equilibrium toward the products but the direction depends on whether the reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
    • Thinking a catalyst affects the equilibrium position but a catalyst speeds up the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally but does not affect the equilibrium position or the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium.
    • Assuming that the equilibrium constant (K) changes with concentration or pressure but the equilibrium constant is only affected by temperature. Changes in concentration, pressure, or volume shift the position of equilibrium but do not change the value of K.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Physical equilibrium occurs when a physical process (such as phase changes, solubility, or dissolution) reaches a state where the forward and reverse processes occur at the same rate, resulting in no net change in the observable properties of the system over time.

Characteristics of physical equilibrium:

  • Dynamic process: The system is in a constant state of change, but there is no net change in the system’s macroscopic properties.
  • Reversible: The process can proceed in both directions, allowing the system to reach equilibrium.
  • Constant conditions: The system remains stable under constant temperature, pressure, and concentration.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing different polymorphs or allotropes in solid-solid equilibria but Some substances can exist in different solid forms (polymorphs) or allotropes (e.g., graphite and diamond for carbon). At equilibrium, these different solid phases may coexist, but each has its own properties and equilibrium conditions (such as temperature and pressure). Misinterpreting the phase behavior or neglecting that different solid forms might have distinct stabilities can lead to incorrect conclusions.
    • Assuming that solids are in equilibrium without considering temperature or pressure effects.
    • Ignoring the temperature dependence of the solubility of gases.
    • Confusing the concepts of partial pressure and mole fraction in a gas-liquid equilibrium.

• At this stage, number of moles of substances produced per second in the forward reaction is equal to the number of moles of substances which disappear per second in the backward reaction.
Active Mass

The term active mass means the concentration of the reactants expressed in moles per litre (molar concentration) or the pressure of the reacting gas in atmosphere. In the case of gases and solutions, the molar concentration means the number of gram molecules present per litre.

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{\text{Number of gram moles of the substance}}{\text{Volume (in liters)}}$

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{Weight of substance(in grams)}{Molecular weight (MM) \times Volume (in L)}$

$\text{Active Mass} = \frac{W \times 1000}{(MM) \times V(mL)}$

Homogeneous Equilibrium:

  • Definition: In homogeneous equilibrium, all the reactants and products are in the same phase (either all gases, all liquids, or all solids).
  • Example: The equilibrium between nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄) in the gas phase:
$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$

Heterogeneous Equilibrium:

  • Definition: In heterogeneous equilibrium, the reactants and products are in different phases (e.g., solid, liquid, or gas).
  • Example: The equilibrium between calcium carbonate ($CaCO_3$) and its decomposition products:
$\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$the

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
The core concept of dissociation in chemical equilibrium revolves around the reversible breakdown of a compound ( molecular substance) into simpler entities like  smaller molecules. This dissociation process occurs in a solution, and the system reaches an equilibrium where the rate of dissociation equals the rate of recombination.

For any chemical equilibrium dissociation always calculate in terms of mole. It is denoted by x.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
• Chemical equilibrium is influenced by changes in concentration, pressure, and temperature, as explained by Le Chatelier's Principle: When a system at equilibrium experiences a disturbance, the system adjusts to partially counteract the disturbance and re-establish equilibrium.

• Le Chatelier's Principle states that when a dynamic equilibrium in a chemical system is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the system will respond by shifting the equilibrium position to counteract the disturbance and partially restore balance.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Any endothermic reaction, the heat energy will appear on the reactant side  of the equation.
ex. $CaCO₃(s) + heat → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)$.

  • Any exothermic reaction, heat is released and appears on the product side (Not reactant side) of the equation.
ex. $CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) + Energy (heat)$

  • Some examples of irreversible reaction:
  • Combustions reactions, Redox reaction, Neutralization reaction, Precipitation Reaction.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Always check whether, deal with a system at equilibrium and use the correct expressions for Q (reaction quotient) or K (equilibrium constant).
  • Be mindful of the units and stoichiometric coefficients in equilibrium expressions.
  • temperature affect equilibrium constant, but pressure and concentration does not affect equilibrium constant.
  • Use appropriate forms for Kp (for gases) and Kc (for concentrations) depending on the system.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• The degree of dissociation (α) is the fraction of the original substance that dissociates. It's usually expressed as a ratio, ranging from 0 to 1 (0<α<1)
    • Percentage dissociation is the degree of dissociation multiplied by 100.
    • In heterogeneous equilibria (where multiple phases are present), the concentrations of pure solids and liquids do not appear in the equilibrium expression. A mistake is including the concentrations of pure solids or liquids, which are effectively constant.
    • When calculating vapour density for a dissociating substance, the observed vapor density is based on the substance's molar mass after dissociation.
    • Vapour density is half the molar mass of a gas, but students sometimes confuse it with molecular mass. The relationship between vapour density and molar mass must be remembered: VD=MM/2.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
• Assuming pressure affects equilibria for all reactions, but pressure only affects gaseous reactions where there is a difference in the number of moles of gas on either side of the equilibrium. If the number of gas molecules is the same on both sides, changing pressure has no effect.
    • Incorrectly assuming that an increase in temperature always shifts equilibrium toward the products but the direction depends on whether the reaction is endothermic or exothermic.
    • Thinking a catalyst affects the equilibrium position but a catalyst speeds up the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions equally but does not affect the equilibrium position or the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium.
    • Assuming that the equilibrium constant (K) changes with concentration or pressure but the equilibrium constant is only affected by temperature. Changes in concentration, pressure, or volume shift the position of equilibrium but do not change the value of K.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing different polymorphs or allotropes in solid-solid equilibria but Some substances can exist in different solid forms (polymorphs) or allotropes (e.g., graphite and diamond for carbon). At equilibrium, these different solid phases may coexist, but each has its own properties and equilibrium conditions (such as temperature and pressure). Misinterpreting the phase behavior or neglecting that different solid forms might have distinct stabilities can lead to incorrect conclusions.
    • Assuming that solids are in equilibrium without considering temperature or pressure effects.
    • Ignoring the temperature dependence of the solubility of gases.
    • Confusing the concepts of partial pressure and mole fraction in a gas-liquid equilibrium.

blocks.title: Law of Mass Action
blocks.text:
• It states that the rate of a chemical reaction is directly proportional to the product of active masses of the reacting substances raised to the power equal to the stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced chemical equation.

for the given equation:

$\huge\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{\mathrm{n}_1}[\mathrm{D}]^{\mathrm{n}_2}}{[\mathrm{A}]^{\mathrm{m}_1}[\mathrm{B}]^{\mathrm{m}_2}}
$

Δ$n_g$=∑(Number of gaseous moles of product –∑ (Number of gaseous moles of reactants)

Key point:

$K = \frac{K_f}{K_b}$

$\text{If } K > 1: $ Equilibrium favors the products (products are more stable).

$\text{If } K < 1: $ Equilibrium favors the reactants (reactants are more stable).

relation between degree of dissociation and vapor density
blocks.text:
Relation in between degree of dissociation and Molecular mass:

$\alpha = \frac{[MW_{th} - MW_{obs}]}{MW_{obs}} \cdot \frac{n_1}{\Delta n_g}$

$\alpha$ = Degree of dissociation

$\text{MW}_{\text{th}}$ = Molecular weight of reactant also called as Theoretical Molecular Weight ($\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$)

$\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$ = Molecular weight of equilibrium mixture ($\text{MW}_{\text{mix}}$)  also called as Observed Molecular Weight ($\text{MW}_{\text{obs}}$)

$\Delta n_g = \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of products} - \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of reactants}$

D = Initial vapour density ( Vapour density of reactant/Theoretical Vapour Density)

d = Vapour density at equilibrium

$\Delta n_g = \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of products} - \sum \text{no. of gaseous moles of reactants}$
